entities.name: Poitiers Cathedral
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Poitiers Cathedral (Cathédrale Saint-Pierre de Poitiers) in western France, begun in the late 12th century (c. 1162 CE) under Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine — the most powerful couple in 12th-century Europe — and completed in the 13th-14th centuries, is one of the finest examples of Angevin Gothic (Plantagenet) architecture in France, distinguished by its distinctive wide nave with three aisles of almost equal height (hall church plan) and its exceptionally well-preserved medieval stained glass windows.

The association with Eleanor of Aquitaine — who was simultaneously Queen of France (to Louis VII) and later Queen of England (to Henry II), the mother of Richard I 'the Lionheart' and King John, and the most powerful woman in 12th-century Europe — makes Poitiers Cathedral a monument intimately connected to one of history's most remarkable dynasties. Eleanor and Henry II funded significant portions of the cathedral, and Poitiers (Eleanor's ancestral capital) was the center of her famous 'Courts of Love' where she patronized troubadour culture.

Poitiers Cathedral's stained glass program — including one of France's oldest rose windows (c. 1162) and the magnificent Crucifixion window — is among the most complete Romanesque-to-Gothic stained glass ensembles surviving in France. The battle of Poitiers (1356) — where the Black Prince captured the French King John II — is historically the most famous event associated with Poitiers, but the cathedral predates it by two centuries and has outlasted all the conflicts that swirled around this strategically important city.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Poitiers Cathedral — built by Henry II and Eleanor of Aquitaine, a monument to Plantagenet cultural patronage, home to France's oldest rose window, and an architectural masterpiece of Angevin Gothic — is one of western France's most historically layered medieval religious monuments.
